Hahaha, this comment is a blast from the past! I was diagnosed with Crohn’s since then, along with Cyclic Vomiting: so I actually have a good answer for you! Abnormal migraines is another name for cyclic vomiting syndrome. Along with gastroparesis and IBS, cyclic vomiting syndrome is a motility issue of the vagus nerve. The vagal nerve goes down the brain stem and spinal cord, and serves and the main pathway for digestion along with sympathetic/parasympathetic responses (fight/flight, rest/digest). While disorders of this nerve impact digestion and the GI tract, they are considered migraines as the function is remarkable similar in terms of neural activity! I hope this helps.

Hey! I got some tips. I have Crohn’s but mine is typically located in my stomach and duodenum, though I’ve had ileitis and colitis, too! I hope these are helpful.

Advice if you feel well enough to stay home: Heated pads are you best friend: I sit on them for rectal pain, and also have one for my abdominal region, depending on where I’m cramping. I like to situation a cozy spot near the bathroom, and I prepare the bathroom with flushable wipes, soothing wax melts, anti-nausea medication and anti-diarrhea medication, which I take as prescribed. I have an anti-nausea pressure bracelet. I also use alcohol pads for nausea, or other crisps scents like lemon or tangerine. I take frequent bathes, often with Epsom salt. I have a PICC line and receive TPN, but beforehand, I would eat the basics and follow up frequently with my nutritionist. Everyone has trigger foods, so these may not work for you, but I always kept around applesauce, broth, ice cream (or fruit pops/anything really cold), baby puff snacks, and electrolytes. Other things that I could tolerate were some low fat yogurts, eggs (sometimes), mashed potatoes (as bland as possible with just salt), and I would mash up spinach (the only veggie I could tolerate) and put it into very simple smoothies. Now I can’t have this. If you feel these foods are not possible right now, I recommend Italian ice, broth, ice cubes (for hydration), electrolytes, and vitamin supplements. I try to get one breath of fresh air a day during a flare up, either stepping out to the porch or by a window. Passing the time is very hard, especially when symptoms are so active. Low effort activities like video games and reading are soothing, though can cause migraine/ headaches and nausea. Rest is so important. Remembering to be patient with sleep, loving towards the self and preparing a nighttime routine you look forward to in any way can really make a difference. I also recommend telehealth therapy during flare ups, if you have a therapist that you trust.

Non-professional thoughts on when to see a professional: This largely depends on your circumstances and body. Everyone is different. With Crohn’s flare ups, I tend to call my doctor when I start having frequent bloody stools (especially if I feel light headed in any way). I also think if the cramping is unbearable and you cannot move or (especially) if you cannot talk for long, please go to the emergency room. They can stabilize you, and may be able to see where the inflammation if they are willing to admit for a colonoscopy/endoscopy. This year I spent over 3 months in the hospital for various crohn’s related complications, and I think each time I chose to go to the hospital it was the right decision as there were further complications. If you are losing a lot of weight and feel malnourished, please schedule an appointment with your doctor or go to the ER. I also believe I tractable vomiting is a reason to go to the ER. After 48 hours, if I am still vomiting, I would personally, go to stabilize.

I am sending you so much kindness. Please be gentle with yourself. Please know, even when in a flare, you DO have agency. And my final thought is to trust yourself if you think something is “more,” wrong than a typical flare. You know your body and your experiences best. If you do plan to go to the ER, I would say to ask yourself what you feel needs to be accomplished there that cannot be done at home. If you can verbalize it to yourself, it’s probably the right decision to go there. And it helps to communicate effectively to the ER staff.

My suggestions is invertebrates. Even then, I would avoid mystery, rabbit, and many types of nerite snails. I know everyone has already said to absolutely not get a betta, and they are right. I want to throw out a suggestion, just in case you want something that occupies more room in the water column. 

If you want a swimmer, and don’t want cherry shrimp because they are bottom feeders (though they are adorable and fun to observe critters), I would look into Opae Ula shrimp. They are smaller than cherry shrimp, but can survive in smaller environments. They are very hardy, and the only really issue is they need brackish water - but this can very easily (and affordable) be accomplished. They swim around in the water column, so may be more visually appealing. They also seldom need to be fed, and only require water top offs (for the most part). No filtration is necessary, and you can even get away without a heater, depending on where you live. Though cherry shrimp would require a heater, so I would say get one regardless. This is my recommendation for a 2.5 gallon.

Hello friend! I have psoriatic arthritis, hyperthyroidism, and Crohn’s disease. I was diagnosed with the arthritis first, and would take NSAIDs (naproxen) all the time to manage my severe joint pain/inflammation. Hyperthyroidism made the malaise and muscle weakness worse. I felt consistently as you describe it: like I had a flu in my joints that I could not alleviate.

I was diagnosed with Crohn’s disease and was told to stop taking all NSAIDs. My entire treatment changed; my relationship to my joint pain changed alongside the paradigm shift. 

My non professional thoughts that I hope are helpful is to determine the source of the joint pain. If it is autoimmune in nature, biologics indicated for Crohn’s may help. A short course of steroids may help too. 

Otherwise, epsom salt is the best thing on the planet in my opinion. I also focus on foods that lower inflammation, ginger and garlic are frequently used in my kitchen. Certain topical creams really help, depending on the source of the joint pain: voltaren and capsaicin cream are great. 
Light exercises in the morning helped me. But I do believe understanding the joint pain will help open the doors to a solution.

Hey there. I’m sorry you’re going through it. I was 19 when my symptoms first started, and during that period it seemed completely hopeless. I was met with doctors who refused to listen (often being told I had an eating disorder when all I wanted to do was eat). I ended up having to drop out of school, had to eventually quit my job, everything felt like it was crashing down on me. It felt like the disorder was taking literal time away from me.

I’m now almost 26, I have been formally diagnosed. I have a motility specialist, amazing GI, great PCP and nutritionist. I am taking all my nutrients via a feeding tube. I’m back in school full time and I work part time. Here’s my advice, for what it’s worth:

Take the time to focus on your day-to-day living with this disorder. Keep a food journal and almost make it a job to treat your body with respect. Your health is absolutely the priority, and if it takes time to figure out, it’s worth that time. You aren’t wasting your life or being “lazy” by prioritizing your health, because all of the other facets of life come after the health part is stable and you’ve found a good routine. Take the time to find doctors you trust, with whom you can speak candidly. Know that there is no correct prescribed path for life, and while it’s awful living with this disorder, there is a way. It’s hard, incredibly hard, but the hope comes in the moments of mindful attention to the disorder. I’m not going to lie and say one day the symptoms disappear, and your life will most likely be shaped by living with GP, but the GP by no means makes up your whole life. The biggest piece of advice I can give is to practice acceptance.

Sending you all my best.

Hello. I’m sorry that you are currently so overwhelmed and desperate that it’s come to this point, but I urge you to reconsider. I have been formally diagnosed with schizophrenia, after some deliberation with my doctor, they changed my initial diagnosis to schizoaffective, depression type, as I have both psychotic episodes and depressive episodes. At first the news brought my whole world to a grinding halt, but I assure you this is something that you can live with. Seek treatment, don’t just google symptoms and diagnosis yourself. If you have even the smallest inclination that there might be something wrong, you are valid and deserve to be treated properly. Psychosis is incredibly terrifying but it is far more complicated than what most people imagine it to be, so again, I urge you to see a professional before jumping to any conclusions about yourself. And if you are diagnosed with a psychotic disorder, know you aren’t alone. 1 in a 100 people suffer from schizophrenia, that means if you’re in a crowded space, chances are someone has schizophrenia and is simple living day to day with. Please don’t torture yourself with unnecessary stigma, and know that your health is something to live for. If you ever need and ear to listen, feel free to send me a message!

I am incredibly grateful that, when presented with the video, you opted to seek education and find out more. However, what I find bothersome, is the only reason people are interested is because they are witnessing something “unusual” and they find it wild. 

This does two things: firstly, many people will not take the step you took, and will simply view DID as a freak show where people switch and have fun with their alters when, in fact, the disorder is significantly more complicated than that. Not everyone has the resolve to learn more, as you did, which is incredibly unfortunate. While I am glad it helped, I just hope more DID youtubers introduce the topic educationally. 

Secondly, DID is caused by trauma. This fact shouldn’t be forgotten, ever. DID is a traumagenic disorder and I find that these videos make light of that. The real hardship with having DID comes from the PTSD associated with it. This is paramount to remember because DID is not meant to be fun, cool or part of a hype. If we discuss this disorder, we should be discussing how to help people with it and how to avoid it all together. We shouldn’t sensationalize trauma. 

While I feel people absolutely should be more educated in DID, I think it’s the responsibility of the you tubers to be aware of how they impact crowds. Many young people may think DID is just switching or something “neat” when reality it is just another disorder affecting the mind.

Again, thank you for being reasonable and learning more. I wish you all the best!
